title: Point of View, Tone and Perspective
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · Reading: Craft and Structure
summary: How to identify the narrator and the author's point of view, read tone and attitude, and separate characters' perspectives in ACT literary narratives, with tone vocabulary, worked examples and a full practice passage.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Point-of-view questions belong to the **Craft and Structure** category (**26–33% of the scored ACT Reading questions**, about 7 to 9 of the 27 scored questions). Every scored ACT Reading section has one **literary narrative** (fiction or memoir), and that passage almost always brings several questions about who is telling the story, how characters see each other, and what feeling the words carry. Informational passages ask about the **author's** point of view and tone too.

rows: "The point of view from which the passage is told is best described as that of:"
Who tells the story and from what moment in time
"Based on the passage, the father views the shop as:" / "The uncle's reply mainly suggests that he:"
What ONE character thinks or feels, from his words and actions
"The author's attitude toward X is best described as:" / "The author would most likely agree that:"
What the writer thinks, from his evaluative words
"The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:"
The feeling carried by the word choice
"Over the course of the passage, the narrator's feelings change from:"
The attitude at the start and at the end

blocks.text: Step 1: Identify the narrator
Ask two questions: **Who is speaking?** and **When is he speaking?**

rows: "I", "my"; the story is about the narrator
Only his own thoughts; guesses about others
"I", but the story is mainly about someone else ("my uncle")
What he saw and what he was told
"he", "she"; we see inside several characters' minds

blocks.text: **Time position** matters just as much. Many ACT narrators are adults looking back. The passage then has two "selves": the **experiencing self** (the boy, who felt things at the time) and the **narrating self** (the adult, who now understands them). Clues: "years later", "I did not understand then", "I later realized", "now", a present-tense ending.

items: ✓ "What I did not understand then was that the shop was failing." → adult narrator who knows more now. ✗ "a boy telling events as they happen" ("then" shows distance in time).
✓ "I thought of it, that first week, as a prison." → the BOY's feeling. ✗ "The narrator believes the shop is a prison." (the adult no longer thinks so)
✓ "She wondered if her brother had noticed" (third person, inside her mind only) → limited. ✗ omniscient (we never enter the brother's mind).

blocks.title: مين بيحكي وإمتى؟
blocks.text: أول حاجة في القصة: الراوي مين؟ (I ولا he/she) وبيحكي إمتى؟ لو لقيت years later أو I did not understand then أو now يبقى ده واحد كبير بيفتكر وهو صغير. ساعتها فرّق بين إحساس الولد وقتها ورأي الراجل دلوقتي.
Step 2: Separate the voices

A passage can contain several points of view: the narrator's, each character's and, in informational texts, the author's and the views of the people he quotes. The ACT often puts one person's view in an answer about another person.

items: **Attach every opinion to its owner.** "Fixing the past" is the father's phrase, not the narrator's adult view.
**Characters reveal themselves by what they say, what they do and how others react.** The uncle never says "I respect every customer"; he shows it by treating every watch the same way.
**In informational passages, quoted people are not the author.** "Critics argue…" gives the critics' view; look for the author's reply ("fairly", "but", "I think").

✓ "The father doubts the shop has a future." (he asks how long his brother will keep "fixing the past") ✗ "The narrator, as an adult, thinks the shop was a waste of time." (that was the boy's side, taken "without thinking")
✓ "The author agrees the critics have a point." ("Critics point out, fairly…") ✗ "The author agrees with the critics completely." ("fairly" accepts one point, not the whole view)

blocks.text: Step 3: Read the tone

Tone is the attitude carried by word choice. To find it, collect the **evaluative words** (words that judge: foolish, generous, careful, sadly, a small pleasure) and ask: positive, negative, neutral or mixed? Then pick the choice that matches the direction AND the strength.

items: admiring / appreciative
shows respect and approval
affectionate
shows warm love
reverent
deeply respectful, almost as for something sacred
nostalgic
longing for the past, sweet and sad together
wistful
quietly sad about something lost or impossible
rueful
regretful, usually about one's own mistake, often with a little humour
wry
dry, quietly amused by a contradiction
ironic
saying one thing but meaning something different, or noting a result opposite to what was expected
ambivalent
pulled in two directions, mixed feelings
detached / objective
no personal feeling shown
skeptical
doubtful, needs more proof
critical
pointing out faults
resentful
bitter about being treated unfairly
sardonic / scornful
mocking, contemptuous (rarely the answer for an ACT author)
defensive
protecting oneself from criticism
earnest
serious and sincere

rows: "I am sorry to say", "less often than I should have"
"It is a generous answer… But it is also a little sad"
facts, numbers, no "I", no judging adjectives

blocks.title: الـ Tone
blocks.text: لم الكلمات اللي فيها حكم أو إحساس. بعدين حدد: إيجابي ولا سلبي ولا مختلط؟ وقوي ولا هادي؟ كُتّاب الـ ACT غالبًا متوازنين، فالاختيارات المتطرفة زي furious أو ecstatic أو contemptuous نادرًا ما تكون صح.
Worked examples

Excerpt 1 (literary narrative):

Nadia counted the steps from the bus stop to the hospital doors: forty-two. She wondered whether her brother, sitting beside her, was counting too, or whether he was simply looking at the pigeons the way he looked at everything, as though nothing could surprise him.
**Worked example 1 — narrator's point of view**
**Question:** The point of view of the excerpt is best described as that of:

items: A) a third-person narrator who follows Nadia's thoughts only.
B) a first-person narrator who is Nadia's brother.
C) a third-person narrator who knows both characters' thoughts equally.
D) Nadia speaking about herself in the first person.

blocks.text: **Answer: A.** The narrator says "she", so it is third person. We know what Nadia counts and wonders, but we only see the brother from outside ("She wondered whether…"). That is limited third person.

items: **B is wrong** — There is no "I" in the excerpt.
**C is wrong** — If the narrator knew the brother's thoughts, Nadia would not need to wonder.
**D is wrong** — Nadia is "she", not "I".

blocks.text:
Excerpt 2 (humanities):

The new museum's architect has been praised for his daring, and the building is certainly impossible to ignore. Whether it is a good place to look at paintings is another matter. Several rooms are so bright that visitors must squint at the canvases, and the curving walls leave little space for anything larger than a postcard.
**Worked example 2 — author's attitude in an informational passage**
**Question:** The author's attitude toward the museum building is best described as:

items: A) enthusiastic approval.
B) impressed by its boldness but doubtful about its usefulness.
C) completely indifferent.
D) angry and insulting.

blocks.text: **Answer: B.** "Certainly impossible to ignore" grants something positive; "another matter" turns to the problems (bright rooms, no space). Mixed tone: impressed + doubtful.

items: **A is wrong** — Half-right: ignores the criticism after "Whether…".
**C is wrong** — Reversed: the author gives detailed opinions, so he cares.
**D is wrong** — Too extreme: the criticism is calm and specific, not insulting.

blocks.text:
Excerpt 3 (literary narrative):

When Karim announced that he would study music, his grandfather said nothing for a long time. Then he went to the cupboard, took down the old oud that no one had played in thirty years, and set it on the table between them without a word.
**Worked example 3 — character's perspective**
**Question:** The grandfather's action most strongly suggests that he:

items: A) disapproves of Karim's decision but is too polite to say so.
B) wants Karim to sell the old instrument.
C) has forgotten how to play the oud.
D) quietly supports Karim's decision.

blocks.text: **Answer: D.** Characters show their views through actions. Giving the young man the family instrument right after his announcement is a silent gesture of support.

items: **A is wrong** — Reversed: the gift does not fit disapproval; the silence before it is thoughtful, not cold.
**B is wrong** — Not supported: nothing suggests selling.
**C is wrong** — Not supported: the excerpt says no one played it, not that he forgot how.

blocks.text:
Excerpt 4 (memoir):

I promised my mother I would write every week from university. I wrote twice in the first month, once in the second, and then, as students do, discovered that a promise can be postponed indefinitely.
**Worked example 4 — tone of a sentence**
**Question:** The tone of the final sentence is best described as:

items: A) angry.
B) proud.
C) wry and self-critical.
D) objective and scientific.

blocks.text: **Answer: C.** The narrator admits he broke his promise, but "as students do" and "postponed indefinitely" make the confession lightly comic. Wry + self-critical.

items: **A is wrong** — Too extreme, and there is no one he is angry at.
**B is wrong** — Reversed: he is admitting a fault, not boasting.
**D is wrong** — The sentence is full of personal feeling and humour, not neutral facts.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Boy vs man.** The choice gives the young narrator's feeling as the adult's view (or the other way round).
**Wrong owner.** One character's words or opinion are attributed to another character or to the author.
**Extreme tone.** furious, ecstatic, contemptuous, completely indifferent: ACT tones are usually moderate.
**Half a mixed tone.** The author praises and then says "but": the answer must include both sides.
**One-sentence tone.** The tone of a paragraph must fit ALL of its clues, not one dramatic word.
**Reading jokes literally.** "A prison with a sea view" is not a real prison, and the narrator is not furious.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: In a literary narrative, note the narrator type (I / he / she) and time clues (then, later, now) during your first read.
Mark whose opinion each strong phrase belongs to.
For tone, collect 2–3 evaluative words, label the direction (positive / negative / mixed) and the strength, then match.
For shift questions, check the first and last appearance of the feeling: both ends must match.
Prefer moderate, two-sided choices ("admiring but doubtful") when the passage contains "but" or "yet".

blocks.text: Practice

Now try a full literary narrative (about 700 words) with 9 questions on narrator, characters' perspectives and tone. It is **untimed**, but aim for about 10 minutes. As you read, separate the boy's feelings from the adult narrator's understanding.

blocks.title: ACT Reading practice — Point of view and tone
blocks.intro: One literary narrative, 9 questions, untimed. Decide who is speaking and when, attach every opinion to its owner, and match both the direction and the strength of the tone.

questions.p:
LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is adapted from a short story. The narrator recalls a summer he spent working in his uncle's shop.

[1] The summer I turned fourteen, my father decided that I had too much free time and too little discipline, and he solved both problems at once by sending me to work in my uncle Fathi's watch repair shop in Alexandria. The shop was a narrow room between a pharmacy and a shop that sold school uniforms, and it was so small that when a customer came in, I had to step outside to make space. I thought of it, that first week, as a kind of prison with a sea view.

[2] My uncle did not seem to notice my suffering. He sat at his bench from nine in the morning until eight at night with a magnifying lens screwed into one eye, bent over the open back of some stranger's watch, and he spoke perhaps twenty words an hour. When he did speak, it was usually to tell me to stop moving. "A watch is a quiet thing," he said on the second day, after I had knocked a tray of tiny screws onto the floor. "It does not like nervous people." I spent the rest of the morning on my knees with a magnet, hating watches and, I am sorry to say, hating him a little too.

[3] What I did not understand then was that the shop was failing. Fewer people wore watches at all, and those who did bought cheap ones that were not worth repairing. My father understood this perfectly well. At dinner he would ask his brother, not unkindly, how long he planned to keep "fixing the past," and my uncle would answer that the past was still ticking, thank you, and ask for the bread. I took my father's side without thinking about it. He was a civil engineer who built roads; he worked in the future. My uncle worked in a room that smelled of oil and old leather, repairing things that most people had already decided to replace.

[4] And yet, slowly and against my will, the room began to interest me. I noticed that my uncle treated every watch the same way, whether it was a gold one brought in by a lawyer or a scratched plastic one carried by a schoolboy who had saved for it. He cleaned each one, oiled each one, and wrote the date of the repair in tiny letters inside the case. When I asked him why he bothered with the cheap ones, he looked at me as though I had asked why he bothered to breathe. "The boy will look at the time on that watch a thousand times," he said. "It should be right a thousand times."

[5] By August he let me open the backs of watches myself. My hands shook at first, and he said nothing, which I later understood was his way of being kind. I learned to hold my breath when I lifted a balance wheel, to work in the morning when the light was good, and to stop when I grew impatient, because impatience was the only tool in the shop that could not be repaired. I did not become good at it. But for the first time in my life I was doing something slowly on purpose.

[6] The shop closed six years later, while I was at university studying engineering, as my father had wished. My uncle sold the benches and the tools to a collector and moved into a flat near the Corniche, where he repaired watches for his neighbours, for free, until his eyes would no longer let him. I visited him there less often than I should have. Young men are busy, or believe they are.

[7] I build bridges now, which my father would have approved of, and I am told I am careful at it, which I think my uncle would have approved of more. On my desk there is a small steel watch that he repaired for me at the end of that summer. Inside the case, in letters I need a magnifying glass to read, is the date. It still keeps good time. I wind it every morning, slowly, the way I was taught.
questions.q: The point of view from which the passage is told is best described as that of:
c: a fourteen-year-old boy describing events as they happen.
an outside narrator who knows the thoughts of every character.
the uncle remembering the last years of his shop.
an adult looking back on a summer from his youth with understanding he did not have then.
questions.e: "The summer I turned fourteen…", "What I did not understand then…" and "I build bridges now" show a grown man telling the story from later. A ignores the past tense and "now"; B is wrong because the narrator is "I", a character; C confuses the narrator with the uncle.

questions.q: The description of the shop as "a kind of prison with a sea view" (paragraph 1) mainly conveys:
c: the adult narrator's belief that his father treated him cruelly.
the boy's feeling of being trapped, described by the older narrator with gentle humour.
the narrator's admiration for the shop's beautiful location.
the uncle's opinion that the shop was too small.
questions.e: "That first week" marks the feeling as the boy's; "prison" shows resentment, and adding "with a sea view" makes the complaint a little comic. A is too extreme and never stated; C ignores "prison"; D gives the view to the wrong character.

questions.q: Based on the passage, the father's attitude toward his brother's shop is best described as:
c: doubtful about its future but not hostile toward his brother.
angry that his brother refused to help the family.
envious of his brother's skill and freedom.
completely uninterested in what his brother did.
questions.e: The father "understood" the shop was failing and teased his brother about "fixing the past", but the narrator stresses "not unkindly". B and C invent emotions the text never shows; D is reversed, since he asks about the shop at dinner.

questions.q: The uncle's reply that "the past was still ticking, thank you" (paragraph 3) mainly suggests that he:
c: agrees that his shop will soon close.
is deeply hurt by his brother's question.
rejects his brother's view with dry good humour.
wants his nephew to become a civil engineer.
questions.e: He turns his brother's phrase into a joke about watches ("still ticking") and calmly asks for the bread: he disagrees, but lightly. A is reversed; B is too extreme for a calm, joking reply; D brings in an idea about the father, not the uncle (wrong character).

questions.q: In paragraph 4, the uncle's explanation of why he repairs cheap watches carefully reveals his belief that:
c: only expensive watches deserve careful repair.
schoolboys should not be trusted with watches.
his nephew asks too many questions.
every owner deserves a watch that works properly, whatever it cost.
questions.e: He treats every watch "the same way" and says the boy's watch "should be right a thousand times": the value is in the owner's use, not the price. A is reversed; B and C are never suggested.

questions.q: The narrator's comment that his uncle's silence when his hands shook was "his way of being kind" (paragraph 5) shows that the narrator:
c: still believes his uncle did not care about him.
came to understand his uncle's behaviour differently later in life.
was frightened of his uncle throughout the summer.
thinks his uncle should have praised him more often.
questions.e: The key words are "I later understood": the boy saw only silence; the adult sees kindness. This change of understanding is typical of a narrator looking back. A is reversed; C ignores the growing interest in paragraph 4; D criticizes the uncle, which the narrator does not do here.

questions.q: The statement "Young men are busy, or believe they are" (paragraph 6) is best described as:
c: rueful self-criticism.
angry blame of his uncle.
neutral reporting of a fact.
proud self-justification.
questions.e: The sentence follows "less often than I should have": the narrator admits a fault, and "or believe they are" shows he now doubts his old excuse. Rueful = regretful in a gentle way. B blames the wrong person; C ignores the regret; D is reversed: he is not defending himself.

questions.q: The narrator's attitude toward his uncle in the final paragraph is best described as:
c: mildly resentful.
indifferent.
affectionate and respectful.

A belongs to the boy in paragraph 2, not the adult; B is reversed by these details; D: nothing suggests he feels sorry for his uncle.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Narrator questions: decide who is speaking (I / he / she) and from what moment in time.
An adult looking back has two selves: the feelings of the young self are not the adult's present view.
Characters show their perspectives through words, actions and other characters' reactions; attach every opinion to its owner.
Tone comes from evaluative words; match the direction (positive, negative, mixed) and the strength.
ACT tones are usually moderate and often mixed: avoid extreme choices.
